fin1-the-head-and-the-tail.reason: Opens on Deuteronomy 28's blessing and loss; who holds the pen (the lender sets covenants, remedies and timing) comes mid-lesson, and the one sentence to write only in the closing lines.
fin1-the-head-and-the-tail.open: THE QUESTION IN THE TITLE. Who holds the pen on your mortgage? The lender does. Deuteronomy 28:44 calls the lender the head and the borrower the tail. That names a position, not a sin: the head sets the covenants, defines the remedy when a payment is missed, and above all controls the timing. Scripture does not forbid borrowing, but it tells you which end Yahweh means you to stand at. Here is how to read it.
fin1-the-head-and-the-tail.example: THE TWO SENTENCES. Say a family carries one mortgage. The first sentence reads: this bank lends to us, we borrow from this bank, so this bank sets the terms if things go wrong. The second reads: this reverses when we hold reserves at a set level and this house is free of its note, by a date we name. The first sentence is honesty. The second is the plan.
fin1-the-head-and-the-tail.close: BACK TO THE QUESTION. Who holds the pen on your mortgage? The lender, the head of the arrangement, who writes the covenants, the remedies and the timing. Seeing that as position rather than shame frees you to plan instead of hide or despair. So write the sentence with real names in it, then write the second one: what must be true, and by when, for the direction to reverse. Keep both written, and you will be neither ashamed of where you stand nor content to stay there.

teen.open: Who is in charge when you borrow money? The lender. Deuteronomy 28 calls the lender the head and the borrower the tail.
teen.close: So the lender holds the pen. Borrowing is not shameful, but it puts you under someone. Make a plan to get to the other end.

senior.open: Deuteronomy 28:44 names the lender the head and the borrower the tail. The title asks who holds the pen on your mortgage, and the passage answers plainly: the lender, as a matter of position rather than shame.
senior.close: So the answer is plain. The lender sets the terms, the remedies and the timing. Write that down with real names, then write what must be true, and by when, for the direction to reverse.

fin2-when-the-money-failed.reason: Walks Genesis 47 stage by stage; the point of the title (the slide is a chain of reasonable steps, visible only on paper beforehand) and the written order arrive late, then it ends on seed and the fifth part.
fin2-when-the-money-failed.open: THE QUESTION IN THE TITLE. How does a written liquidation order expose the slide before it starts? In Genesis 47, Egypt lost its land through a chain of reasonable trades: money, then livestock, then land and labour. No step was foolish, yet the chain ended in servitude. Such a slide is invisible from the inside. The only place to see it in time is on paper, beforehand, while nothing is yet wrong. Here is how the chapter shows it.
fin2-when-the-money-failed.example: A HOUSEHOLD'S CHAIN. Say income stops for a year. First the emergency reserve goes, which is reasonable. Then the equipment, which is reasonable. Then a loan against the property, which is reasonable. Then harsher terms to keep from losing it, which is reasonable too. Written down beforehand, the list shows where it ends. So the family marks stage two as the point to do something different: sell sooner, ask for help early, or change the income instead of financing the gap.
fin2-when-the-money-failed.close: BACK TO THE QUESTION. How does a written order expose the slide? It lays out, ahead of time, the chain of reasonable trades that ended with Egypt owning nothing. Read it backwards and you see where it leads. Then mark the stage where you will make a different move instead of the next trade, because a decision at stage two is a strategy and the same decision at stage four is a rescue. Your reserves can run out, but your choices need not.

teen.open: How can writing a list protect you from losing everything? It shows the slide before it starts, so each small, sensible step does not lead you somewhere bad.
teen.close: So write the list while things are fine. Mark the point where you will do something different. That keeps you choosing instead of sliding.

senior.open: Genesis 47 shows a nation surrendering its land in reasonable stages, with no fraud anywhere. The title asks how a written liquidation order helps, and the answer is that it reveals the chain while it can still be broken.
senior.close: So the answer is plain. Write the order of what you would sell, read it backwards, and mark the stage where you will act differently. A decision made early is a strategy; made late, it is only a rescue.

fin3-they-shall-rise-up-suddenly.reason: Opens on Habakkuk's thick clay; the dates that can catch you (rate reset, balloon, covenant test, renewal, demand clause) and the warning against trusting quiet months come mid-lesson; ends on the woe.
fin3-they-shall-rise-up-suddenly.open: THE QUESTION IN THE TITLE. Which date could catch you off guard? Not the monthly payment. The dangerous ones are the rate reset, the balloon or maturity, the covenant test, the renewal, and the demand clause. The risk sits on those dates, not spread through the calm months between. Habakkuk 2:7 warns that the creditor rises up suddenly: he was there all along, only not moving. Here is how the Word warns against trusting the calm.
fin3-they-shall-rise-up-suddenly.example: ONE PAGE OF DATES. Say a household has a loan whose rate resets next spring with sixty days' notice. Beside that date they write the action: refinance with this lender, or sell this asset, or draw on this reserve. Then they see the refinance would take ninety days. That gap is the real exposure, and it is a timing problem they can still fix while everything is quiet.
fin3-they-shall-rise-up-suddenly.close: BACK TO THE QUESTION. Which date could catch you off guard? Whichever scheduled date you have not written down, with its notice period and your action beside it. Thirty-six good months prove nothing about the thirty-seventh, because the danger sits on known dates. Habakkuk's word is suddenly. So list every date your financing can change, and fix any action that takes longer than the notice you would receive. A household that knows its dates is not caught by the calm.

teen.open: Which day could surprise you on a loan? Not the regular payment. It is the days when the deal can change, like when the rate resets.
teen.close: So do not trust the quiet months. Write down the dates that matter, and plan what you would do before they come.

senior.open: A loan changes state on particular dates: the rate reset, the maturity, the covenant test, the renewal, the demand clause. The title asks which could catch you off guard, and Habakkuk warns against reading quiet months as safety.
senior.close: So the answer is plain. The dangerous date is any you have not listed with its notice period and your planned action. Prepare while things are calm, because the creditor rises up suddenly.

fin4-the-wicked-borroweth-and-payeth-not.reason: Answers early (the fault is payeth not again, not the borrowing) and ends on unpaid intention, but the open hand the title promises is taught mid-lesson and not landed at the end.
fin4-the-wicked-borroweth-and-payeth-not.close: BACK TO THE QUESTION. Is your debt really the sin? No. Psalm 37:21 judges the obligation that stops being honoured, not the borrowing, and sets the righteous opposite the wicked as one who shows mercy and gives, a lender at the end of the psalm (Psalms 37:21, 26). So list every obligation, formal and informal, and remove the mark on any you have quietly stopped intending to pay. Then keep walking toward the open hand.

teen.open: Is owing money a sin? Psalm 37:21 says the wrong is not paying back, not borrowing.
teen.close: So the debt itself is not the sin. Not meaning to pay it back is. Keep your word, and learn to give with an open hand.

senior.open: Psalm 37:21 is often used to call debt sin, yet its condemning phrase is that the wicked pays not again. The fault lies in the abandoned obligation.
senior.close: So the answer is plain. Borrowing is not the sin; quietly ceasing to intend repayment is. Settle that intention this week, and walk toward the merciful, giving life the psalm describes.

fin5-what-hast-thou-in-the-house.reason: Opens on the widow's debt; the answer (the thing you call nothing, worked with your own hands, paid the debt and kept providing) builds through the story and is only named for the reader in the closing lines.
fin5-what-hast-thou-in-the-house.open: THE QUESTION IN THE TITLE. What is already in your house? Usually the thing you call nothing. The widow said she had nothing but a pot of oil, and that pot paid her debt and kept her family living (2 Kings 4:2, 7). The answer was not another loan. It was what she already held, worked with her own hands, with capacity gathered first. Here is how the account shows it.
fin5-what-hast-thou-in-the-house.close: BACK TO THE QUESTION. What is already in your house? Something you have been calling nothing: a trade, a licence, a vehicle standing still, a room, a machine, an unclaimed hour. The widow's oil paid the debt and then let her live of the rest, production rather than a better arrangement. So write yours down, take the smallest real step to a first dollar this month, and gather your empty vessels, because her preparation set the measure of her provision.

teen.open: What do you already have that could help? The widow thought she had nothing but a little oil, and it paid her debt.
teen.close: So look again at what you have, like a skill or a tool. Take one small step to use it this month.

senior.open: The prophet asked the widow what she had in the house, and she named a pot of oil as almost nothing. The title asks what is in yours, and the account answers: the asset you have overlooked.
senior.close: So the answer is plain. Most households hold something they call nothing. Name it, take one real step to make it produce, and prepare well, for her provision was bounded by the vessels she gathered.

fin7-alas-for-it-was-borrowed.reason: Locates the man's grief early, but what caring for a borrowed thing actually looks like (maintaining financed assets, telling the truth early) arrives mid-lesson; the self-test only in the final lines.
fin7-alas-for-it-was-borrowed.open: THE QUESTION IN THE TITLE. Are you caring for what you only borrowed? The man whose axe head sank grieved first that it belonged to someone else (2 Kings 6:5). A financed asset is partly another's. Caring for it means the upkeep, insurance and service you owe it even when nobody is watching, and telling the owner the truth early when something goes wrong. Here is how the account shows it.
fin7-alas-for-it-was-borrowed.close: BACK TO THE QUESTION. Are you caring for what you only borrowed? You are if you treat a financed thing the way the man treated the axe head: you remember whose it is, you keep it up, and you report trouble early instead of hiding it. The mercy came after his honesty, and he still reached for it himself. So name the one asset you have begun treating as already paid off, and do this month the care a man who remembered would have done.

teen.open: Do you take care of things that are not fully yours? The man who lost the axe head was upset because it was borrowed.
teen.close: So care for borrowed things as if the owner is watching. If something goes wrong, tell the truth right away.

senior.open: When the axe head sank, the man's first words were that it was borrowed. The title asks whether we care for what we only borrowed, and every financed asset puts that question to us.
senior.close: So the answer turns on conduct. Keep up what is partly another's, keep the required insurance, and report trouble early. Name the asset you have neglected, and give it the care it is owed this month.

fin8-he-frankly-forgave-them-both.reason: Sets the scene at Simon's table; the answer (one who knows how much was cancelled loves much, and cannot treat a debtor harshly) arrives late, after the course recap; ends on two columns.
fin8-he-frankly-forgave-them-both.open: THE QUESTION IN THE TITLE. Why should a cancelled debt change how you treat those who owe you? Because the one forgiven much loves much (Luke 7:42-43). Before Yahweh every one of us had nothing to pay, and was forgiven fully. A man who truly knows the size of what was cancelled for him cannot handle a brother's small debt harshly. Here is how Jesus shows it at Simon's table.
fin8-he-frankly-forgave-them-both.close: BACK TO THE QUESTION. Why should a cancelled debt change how you treat those who owe you? Because the size of what you know was forgiven sets how much you love. Simon reckoned his debt small and loved little; the woman knew hers was great and loved much. So write both columns: what you would owe if everything came due with nothing to pay, and how you are treating those who owe you. If the columns do not match, the second one is what needs to change.

teen.open: Why should being forgiven change how you treat others? Jesus says the person forgiven much loves much.
teen.close: So remember how much you have been forgiven. Then be gentle with people who owe you.

senior.open: In Luke 7 Jesus tells of a creditor who forgave two debtors who had nothing to pay. The title asks why a cancelled debt should change us, and His answer is that the forgiven one loves.
senior.close: So the answer is plain. Those who know how much was forgiven them cannot deal harshly with their own debtors. Compare honestly what you were released from with how you are treating those who owe you.

fin6-usury-and-who-your-brother-is.reason: Answers early (same loan, no increase to a brother in need, lawful interest to a stranger) but ends on the blessing clause, not on naming who is across the table before the money moves.
fin6-usury-and-who-your-brother-is.close: BACK TO THE QUESTION. Who is across the table, and does it change the price? Yes, it does. To a brother in need, you lend with no increase, because pricing his trouble takes profit from it. To a commercial party, interest is lawful and the terms are written (Deuteronomy 23:19-20). Most harm comes from never saying which kind of loan it is. So name the category aloud before the money moves, and trust Yahweh to bless the work of your hands.

teen.open: Does it matter who you lend money to? Yes. The Word says do not charge interest to a brother in need.
teen.close: So before you lend, say out loud what kind of loan it is. A brother in need gets help without extra charge.

senior.open: Deuteronomy 23 forbids interest to a brother yet permits it to a stranger. The title asks whether the person across the table changes the price, and the law answers yes.
senior.close: So the answer is plain. A brother's need is not priced; a commercial loan carries real, written terms. Name which kind it is before the money moves, and Yahweh ties His blessing to that obedience.
